planting.note: Root stem cuttings with at least one node in moist sphagnum or chunky aroid mix; give a moss pole or bark slab early so the climbing habit and full leaf lobing develop.

directions: Radiatum philodendron is a climbing hemiepiphyte from Mexico and Central America whose juvenile leaves are simple and heart-shaped but mature into deeply, irregularly lobed foliage that reads almost fenestrated, giving it a lacy, Monstera-like silhouette without true perforations. It climbs by aerial roots on bark or moss poles, with leaf size and lobing increasing noticeably as the plant gains height and maturity. Bright, filtered light and consistent moisture in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix keep growth vigorous; it differs from the similarly lobed Philodendron pedatum by its broader, more irregular lobe pattern and stouter growth habit. Provide humidity above 50% and avoid letting the mix dry out completely between waterings.

planting.note: Propagate from stem cuttings with a node in warm, humid conditions; young plants root readily in moist chunky mix or sphagnum.

directions: Sagittifolium philodendron is a robust hemiepiphyte native to Mexico and Central America, named for its large, glossy, arrow-shaped (sagittate) leaves that can reach two feet or more on mature plants. Young plants begin as a low, terrestrial rosette before sending climbing stems upward once they encounter a support, at which point leaf size and the depth of the basal lobes both increase. It tolerates a wider range of indoor light than many velvet-leaf collector species and grows steadily in bright, indirect light with regular watering. Distinguish it from the similarly shaped but smaller-leaved Philodendron bipennifolium by its thicker leaf texture and more pronounced, rounded basal lobes.

planting.note: Take single-node stem cuttings and root in warm, humid conditions; provide a textured climbing support early since aerial root attachment slows on smooth surfaces.

directions: Ornatum philodendron is a climbing species from Trinidad and northern South America best identified by its petioles, which are studded with small, soft, wart-like protrusions rather than being smooth like most climbing philodendrons. Elongated, narrow, glossy leaves emerge coppery-bronze and mature to deep green, held on a vigorous vine that clings readily to bark or moss poles with aerial roots. It prefers bright, indirect light and a chunky, well-aerated aroid mix that dries slightly between waterings. The textured petiole is the clearest way to separate it from smooth-stemmed look-alikes such as Philodendron hastatum.

planting.note: Propagate from stem cuttings; establishes quickly as a groundcover or trained climber in frost-free landscapes.

directions: Florida Green philodendron is a hybrid selection (Philodendron pedatum x squamiferum) widely planted as a shade groundcover and foundation plant across South Florida and other frost-free regions. Deeply, irregularly lobed, glossy dark-green leaves are held on a semi-climbing vine that sprawls as groundcover when unsupported or ascends trees and structures given a support. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of light from partial shade to filtered sun, making it a durable landscape workhorse rather than a delicate collector plant. It is the parent of the paler-veined 'Florida Ghost' and the coarser-leaved, deep-burgundy-new-growth 'Florida Beauty', both already documented in this dataset.

planting.note: Propagate from stem cuttings; grows fastest in warm, humid, partially shaded landscape beds or large containers.

directions: Florida Improved philodendron is a vigorous selection out of the 'Florida Green' lineage, bred for larger, more deeply cut leaves and faster coverage in commercial landscape settings. The semi-climbing vine produces broad, dark-green, heavily lobed foliage that is noticeably bigger per leaf than standard 'Florida Green', giving a bolder textural statement in mass plantings. It handles heat and humidity well and performs as either a sprawling groundcover in shade or a trained climber on a support in brighter partial sun. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil and water regularly during active growth, allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings in cooler months.

common_name: El Choco Red Philodendron (Red-Backed Climbing Philodendron)

planting.note: Root single-node stem cuttings in moist sphagnum; provide a moss pole from an early stage to encourage larger, more colorful mature leaves.

directions: El Choco Red philodendron is a South American collector hybrid climbing species grown primarily for the vivid burgundy-red undersides and petioles that contrast with its glossy, dark-green upper leaf surface. New growth emerges in warm coppery-red tones before the upper surface darkens to green while the reverse retains its saturated red color, a trait best developed under bright, indirect light. As a hemiepiphyte, it climbs steadily on a moss pole or bark, producing progressively larger leaves with age and support. Keep the chunky aroid mix evenly moist but never soggy, and maintain humidity above 50% to prevent leaf-edge browning.

planting.note: Root single-node cuttings that include at least some variegated leaf tissue in water or moist sphagnum to preserve the pattern in new growth.

directions: Gabby philodendron is a compact, slower-growing variegated sport within the heartleaf philodendron group, distinguished by smaller leaves marbled with irregular cream and soft-green patches and a shorter internode habit than its faster-growing relative 'Brasil'. It trails or climbs gently on a small support, staying tidy and well suited to hanging baskets or tabletop pots rather than covering large areas quickly. Bright, indirect light is essential to sustain the pale variegation, since low light causes new leaves to revert toward solid green. Allow the top inch of potting mix to dry between waterings and avoid direct sun, which can scorch the thin cream sectors.
